entities.name: Annales Veteris Testamenti
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The *Annales Veteris Testamenti, a Prima Mundi Origine Deducti* ('Annals of the Old Testament, Deduced from the First Origins of the World') is a monumental 1650 scholarly work by James Ussher (1581–1656), the Anglican Archbishop of Armagh and Primate of All Ireland. Representing the zenith of biblical chronology, Ussher's *Annales* meticulously calculated the timeline of Earth's history from creation to the destruction of the Second Temple, aiming to synchronize biblical narratives with secular history. This comprehensive project provided a precise, date-stamped framework for understanding human existence, profoundly influencing historical thought in the Protestant world for centuries.

Ussher's methodology was an exhaustive synthesis of scriptural and historical sources. He cross-referenced the Hebrew Bible (Masoretic Text), the Septuagint, the Samaritan Pentateuch, and numerous ancient historical texts, including the works of Josephus and early Church Fathers. Through intricate calendrical and genealogical computations, Ussher famously pinpointed the creation of the world to the eve of Sunday, October 23, 4004 BC. The *Annales* detailed every significant event, from the lives of patriarchs and kings to the dates of major biblical floods and exiles, presenting a seamless chronological narrative that spanned millennia.
